opus-5.5.text:
I think the first filter for me is hardware efficiency. There are a lot of beautiful ideas in the old literature, from classical online learning, adaptive filtering, and associative memory research in the eighties and nineties. Most of them were never designed with GPUs in mind. So when I look at an old algorithm, the first thing I ask is: can this be parallelized? Can I rewrite it so that most of the computation becomes matrix multiplications that run well on tensor cores? If the answer is no, then no matter how elegant it is, it's very hard to scale to billions of parameters and trillions of tokens.

The delta rule is a good example. It goes back to Widrow and Hoff, the least mean squares algorithm, around 1960. People had already noticed that linear attention is basically a fast weight programmer, an outer-product memory, and that adding the delta rule should make the memory better, because instead of only adding new associations you also correct old ones. The idea was known. What blocked it was that the recurrence looked inherently sequential, so training was slow. Much of our work on DeltaNet was finding a chunkwise parallel form, using things like the WY representation for products of Householder matrices from numerical linear algebra, so training becomes efficient. Once that worked, the old idea suddenly became practical.

The second filter is whether the algorithm has a clear interpretation as optimizing some objective online. I find it useful to view many recurrent models as doing test-time regression: the hidden state is a memory, and each update is one step of an optimizer on a key-value regression loss. From that angle, vanilla linear attention optimizes a fairly naive objective, while the delta rule is like online gradient descent on squared error. That gives you a principled design space. You can ask: what if I add a forgetting term, giving something like gated DeltaNet? What about a better optimizer or a more expressive memory? Historical algorithms that fit this framework are attractive because you can reason about what they should be good at, such as associative recall or state tracking, before running experiments.

The third thing is empirical signal on small, targeted tasks. Synthetic benchmarks like multi-query associative recall, or state-tracking tasks related to formal language theory, are cheap to run and often tell you quickly whether an idea addresses a real weakness of existing architectures. If an old algorithm fixes a known failure mode there, and it's hardware friendly, then it's worth scaling up.

So in short: expressiveness, a clean theoretical story, and above all, whether you can make it fast. In my experience the last one is where most of the real work is, and it's also where old ideas tend to get stuck.

r001.rationale: The response says the first filter is hardware efficiency and asks whether an old algorithm can be parallelized and rewritten as matrix multiplications that run well on tensor cores.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because honestly most of what I work on is not new. Linear attention goes back to 2020, and the ideas behind it, fast weights, associative memory, delta rule learning, those are from the eighties and nineties. So the question is really: why did these things not work then, and what changed?

My first filter is whether the algorithm has a clean mathematical form that I can map onto what hardware is actually good at. A lot of beautiful ideas from the RNN era die at this step. If the recurrence is inherently sequential with a nonlinearity in the state transition, you cannot parallelize it over the sequence length, and then it doesn't matter how elegant it is, you will never train it at the scale where it matters. So when I look at something like the delta rule, the first thing I ask is, can I write this as a chunkwise computation where most of the work becomes matrix multiplications? If yes, that's a very strong signal. If I can get it onto tensor cores, I know I can at least run a fair comparison against softmax attention.

The second filter is whether the algorithm addresses a real failure mode of what we already have. Vanilla linear attention has a very specific problem: the state only accumulates, it never forgets or corrects. You can see this concretely on retrieval tasks, the model gets confused when the same key maps to different values over time. So when I go back to the literature, I'm not browsing randomly, I'm looking for a mechanism that fixes a specific thing. Gating fixes forgetting. The delta rule fixes the overwrite problem, because it's essentially doing one step of online gradient descent on the memory. That framing, the state as a tiny model being trained at test time, turned out to be very productive, and it connected a lot of threads that looked separate before.

The third thing, and this is more taste than principle, is that I like algorithms that compose. If a trick only works in isolation and breaks when you add gating, or when you scale the state size, I lose interest. The ones that survive are usually the ones where the components have clear roles: this part controls memory decay, this part controls what gets written, this part controls how strongly to overwrite. Then you can mix and match and reason about what each change does.

And finally I'd say, I try not to be too romantic about history. Some old ideas were abandoned for good reasons. Others were abandoned because the hardware and the data weren't there. The job is partly archaeology, but mostly it's engineering: write the kernel, run the scaling curve, and see if the idea actually earns its place.

r001.rationale: The response says it selects algorithms that can map to practical hardware, emphasizing sequence parallelization, matrix multiplications, and tensor cores.

astra-6.text:
I usually start with the problem the algorithm was designed to solve. Was it trying to compress a history into a small state, retrieve information efficiently, or update an estimate as new observations arrive? Those problems are closely related to what we ask a language model to do, so they can be useful starting points.

Then I ask whether the algorithm’s assumptions are too restrictive. A classical algorithm might use a fixed update rule or a particular notion of similarity. Can we make those components learnable while preserving the property that made the algorithm attractive—say, efficient memory use or incremental updates?

The other question is whether it runs efficiently on modern hardware. A method can have very good asymptotic complexity and still be slow because its operations are sequential or move too much data. For language models, you need to think about training and inference together.

So I’m looking for a useful computational principle, a way to make it expressive, and an efficient implementation. Then experiments have to tell us whether that combination actually works. The historical connection gives you a hypothesis; it doesn’t guarantee a good architecture.

r001.rationale: The response treats efficient execution on modern hardware as a selection criterion and notes that sequential operations can make an algorithm slow, conveying the relevance of parallel execution.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start with the problem the algorithm was designed to solve, rather than how old or famous it is. Does it offer a useful way to handle memory, compress information, or learn dependencies over long sequences? Then I’d ask whether that idea still makes sense at the scale of language modeling.

There are really two tests. One is about modeling: can the architecture represent the information we need, and can we train it reliably? The other is computational: can we implement it efficiently on modern hardware? An algorithm can have beautiful theoretical complexity and still be slow because it requires too much sequential computation or data movement.

So I’d extract the core idea, build a small version, and compare it against a strong baseline under a fair compute budget. Historical algorithms are a source of hypotheses. What earns them a place in a modern architecture is evidence that they improve the tradeoff between quality and cost.

r001.rationale: The response makes efficient implementation on modern hardware a selection test and warns that excessive sequential computation can make an algorithm slow, communicating the value of parallel execution on practical hardware.
